title: Poisoning LLM-Induced Rule Repositories via Indirect Prompt Injection

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to demonstrate the existence of a poisoning attack surface during the induction phase of LLM-based log parsing. None of the prior papers explicitly establish this specific empirical relationship or attack surface. While papers like [7], [9], [11], [21], and [30] discuss vulnerabilities in in-context learning or backdoor attacks, they do not focus on the induction phase of LLM-based log parsing or demonstrate poisoning attacks in this specific context. Similarly, papers like [8] and [20] explore adversarial attacks on log parsers but do not address the induction phase of LLM-based log parsing.

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism involves injecting indirect prompt injection payloads into induction examples. Papers like [7], [9], [11], [21], and [30] discuss poisoning attacks in the context of in-context learning, where malicious examples are injected to manipulate LLM behavior. These mechanisms are substantively equivalent to the described mechanism, as they involve poisoning the input examples to alter the model's behavior during inference. The specific focus on induction examples in log parsing does not break equivalence, as the underlying primitive (poisoning via example injection) remains the same.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves testing the attack across three Loghub datasets and four poisoning budgets, measuring parsing accuracy drops. Papers like [17] and [13] use Loghub datasets for benchmarking log parsing techniques, and papers like [7], [9], [21], and [30] evaluate poisoning attacks by measuring performance degradation under varying attack budgets. The evaluation design (benchmarking parsing accuracy under poisoning conditions) is substantively equivalent to prior work, even though the specific datasets and metrics differ.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM-based log parsing. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [13], and [17] all address LLM-based log parsing as an application area. While this contribution targets a specific sub-problem (poisoning attacks during induction), the general domain of LLM-based log parsing is well-covered by prior work.

The purpose of the contribution is to determine the most effective payload format for prompt injection attacks. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish the same empirical relationship (i.e., comparing the effectiveness of different payload formats). While several papers discuss prompt injection attacks (e.g., [2], [14], [18], [20]), their focus is on attack mechanisms, defenses, or benchmarks, not on systematically identifying the most effective payload format. The mechanism of systematically comparing payload formats is not present in any prior work.

This evaluation design is not novel. For example, [18] introduces a framework for formalizing and benchmarking prompt injection attacks, which includes systematic evaluations of attack effectiveness. Similarly, [20] introduces a benchmark for indirect prompt injection attacks, which involves evaluating attack success rates under different conditions. These prior works use comparable evaluation designs (e.g., systematic benchmarking of attack effectiveness), even if the specific payload formats or metrics differ.

### Domain
The domain is prompt injection attacks on large language models (LLMs). This domain is extensively covered in prior work, including [2], [14], [18], [20], and others. While this contribution may target specific payload formats, the general application area of prompt injection attacks on LLMs is well-established.

The contribution's mechanism is "canary-based admission control."
